Here's the diff, grouped, with RFC 9457 section numbers.

One thing to know up front: RFC 9457's own Appendix D lists only three changes (the registry, multiple-problem handling, non-dereferenceable type URIs). The text contains more than that, so the list below is from reading both documents, not from Appendix D.

## New registry

**§4.2 "Registered Problem Types"** creates the "HTTP Problem Types" IANA registry for common, widely used type URIs. Policy is Specification Required (RFC 8126 §4.6). The designated expert weighs community feedback and how well-defined the type is; vendor-, application- and deployment-specific values cannot be registered. Registrations may use the prefix `https://iana.org/assignments/http-problem-types#`, and those URIs may not resolve. A four-field template is given (Type URI, Title, Recommended HTTP status code, Reference).

**§4.2.1 "about:blank"** turns RFC 7807's informal "Predefined Problem Types" section into a formal registration: Title "See HTTP Status Code", Recommended HTTP status code "N/A", Reference RFC 9457. The semantics of about:blank are unchanged.

**§6 IANA Considerations** is now a short statement that IANA updated the existing `application/problem+json` and `application/problem+xml` registrations to point at this document, and created the registry. RFC 7807 §6.1 and §6.2 carried full media type registration templates; those are gone from the body.

## Changed requirements

**§3.1** adds a new MUST: if a member's value type doesn't match the specified type, the member MUST be ignored and processing continues as if it were absent. RFC 7807 had no such rule.

**§3.1.1** tightens the type identifier rule. RFC 7807 said consumers MUST use the "type" string as the primary identifier; 9457 says the type URI *after resolution, if necessary*. It also upgrades documentation from "this specification encourages" to a SHOULD: if the type URI is a locator, dereferencing it SHOULD provide human-readable documentation. Consumers SHOULD NOT automatically dereference, now with a carve-out for tools that show information to developers.

**§3.1.1** adds a RECOMMENDED that absolute URIs be used in "type", and that relative URIs include the full path (e.g. `/types/123`), with a worked example of two resources resolving the same relative reference to different URIs.

**§3.1.5** adds the same RECOMMENDED for "instance" (absolute URIs preferred, full path when relative), plus new semantics: a dereferenceable instance URI can be fetched to get the problem details object, possibly in other formats via proactive negotiation; a non-dereferenceable one is an opaque unique identifier.

**§3** adds a RECOMMENDED for multiple problems of different types: represent the most relevant or urgent one. RFC 7807 instead pointed at 207 Multi-Status for encapsulating multiple status messages; that suggestion is gone, and 9457 says generic "batch" problem types don't map well into HTTP semantics.

**§2** is renamed "Requirements Language" and moves to BCP 14 (RFC 2119 plus RFC 8174), with the all-capitals-only condition and "NOT RECOMMENDED" added to the keyword list.

**§3.2** adds a naming constraint: extension names will need to conform to the XML `Name` rule (XML §2.3) to be usable in the XML format. It also drops RFC 7807's claim that new "standard" members can't be defined without defining a new media type.

## New guidance

**§1** adds content negotiation guidance: problem details content can be negotiated with proactive negotiation (HTTP §12.1), and human-readable strings with Accept-Language (HTTP §12.5.4), with the caveat that negotiation may still return a non-preferred default. Also new: problem details work with any status code but most naturally fit 4xx and 5xx.

**§3** adds full request/response examples (POST /purchase, POST /details) and a note that a server may return `application/problem+json` even when the client didn't list it in Accept, as HTTP §12.5.1 allows. The validation example is rewritten: 422 Unprocessable Content instead of 400, and an `errors` array of objects pairing `detail` with a JSON Pointer into the request content.

**§3.1.1** explicitly permits non-resolvable type URIs, with a `tag:` URI example, and argues for resolvable ones anyway: switching later creates a new identity for the problem type and is a breaking change.

**§4.1** now tells designers to look in the registry (§4.2) for an existing type URI before minting one. RFC 7807's closing "In summary: an instance URI will always identify a specific occurrence..." paragraph is removed.

**Appendix A** is new: a non-normative JSON Schema (draft 2020-12) for problem objects, with the text of the spec prevailing on disagreement.

## Renumbering and references

XML moved from Appendix A to Appendix B, "Using Problem Details with Other Formats" from B to C, and Appendix D is the new changes list. Normative references now point at RFC 9110 (HTTP Semantics) instead of RFC 7230/7231, RFC 8259 instead of RFC 7159, RFC 8288 instead of RFC 5988, and the WHATWG HTML living standard instead of the W3C HTML5 REC. RFC 8126, RFC 8174, RFC 6901, RFC 4151 and a JSON Schema draft are added.

## What did not change

The XML namespace is still `urn:ietf:rfc:7807`, both media types are unchanged, and the JSON Schema in Appendix A is still titled "An RFC 7807 problem object".
